title: Sutra on the Deep Kindness of Parents

source.text: Sutra on the Deep Kindness of Parents: selections from the introduction, the ten kindnesses and their verses, and the ways to repay them
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

bm01.heading: The Buddha Bows to Dry Bones by the Road
bm01.plain: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha with a great assembly of thirty-eight thousand monks and many bodhisattvas. The World-Honored One led the assembly south, and by the roadside he saw a heap of bones. The Tathāgata threw his whole body to the ground before those dry bones and bowed in reverence.
bm01.commentary: The sutra opens with this astonishing scene: the Buddha, teacher of the three realms, makes a full prostration before a heap of nameless bones. The disciples' surprise becomes the question this sutra answers.

bm02.heading: They May Have Been Parents in Some Past Life
bm02.plain: Ānanda joined his palms and said: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is the great teacher of the three realms and the compassionate father of all living beings, revered by everyone. Why do you bow to dry bones?" The Buddha said to Ānanda: "This heap of dry bones may have been my ancestors in past lives, or my parents over many lives. For this reason I bow to them now."
bm02.commentary: In the endless cycle of birth and death, every being may at some time have been our parent. The answer carries the thought that no life may be treated lightly.

bm03.heading: A Mother's Bones Are Dark and Light
bm03.plain: The Buddha said to Ānanda: "… While a woman lives, she bears and raises sons and daughters. Each time she gives birth she loses three pecks and three pints of clotted blood, and the child drinks eight bushels and four pecks of white milk. That is why her bones are dark and light."
bm03.commentary: In the omitted passage, the Buddha has Ānanda sort the bones into two piles: white, heavy bones and dark, light ones. The dark, light ones are mothers' bones, because they gave all their blood and strength in bearing and nursing children. It is not a scientific claim but a metaphor that lets us feel a mother's sacrifice in the body.

bm04.heading: First, the Kindness of Carrying and Protecting
bm04.plain: First, the kindness of carrying the child and protecting it. Through heavy bonds of many kalpas, the child now dwells in the mother's womb. Month by month the organs form; week by week the senses open. Her body grows heavy as a mountain; every move feels like a storm. Fine clothes no longer fit, and dust gathers on her mirror.
bm04.commentary: The ten kindnesses are the heart of this sutra. The first is the mother's hardship in carrying the child for ten months. It pictures a mother with no time to adorn herself, guarding only the child within.

bm05.heading: Second, the Kindness of Suffering in Childbirth
bm05.plain: Second, the kindness of suffering at childbirth. Ten months have passed and the hard birth draws near. Each morning feels like grave illness, each day her mind grows dim. Her fear is beyond words; tears of worry soak her breast. Grieving, she tells her family she fears only that death will come.
bm05.commentary: In the past, giving birth meant risking one's life. A mother welcomed her child while carrying the fear of death.

bm06.heading: Third, the Kindness of Forgetting Worry at the Birth
bm06.plain: Third, the kindness of forgetting all worry once the child is born. The day your mother bore you, her insides felt torn apart; body and mind fainted away, and blood poured out. Hearing afterward that the child was healthy, her joy was twice what it had ever been. When the joy settled the pain returned, piercing to the core.
bm06.commentary: Even in such great pain, a single phrase, "the child is healthy," makes her forget every worry. This verse shows what a mother's love is.

bm07.heading: Fourth, the Kindness of Swallowing the Bitter and Giving the Sweet
bm07.plain: Fourth, the kindness of swallowing the bitter and giving the child the sweet. Parents' kindness is deep and weighty; their care and tenderness never cease. They give the sweet without pause and swallow the bitter without a frown. Their love is so deep it is hard to bear, their kindness so deep it is all the more tender. As long as the child is full, the mother does not mind going hungry.
bm07.commentary: This reflects old ways of child-rearing, when a mother chewed food soft to feed her child. Parents give the good things to the child and keep the hard things for themselves.

bm08.heading: Fifth, the Kindness of Taking the Wet Place and Giving the Dry
bm08.plain: Fifth, the kindness of laying the child in the dry place while lying in the wet place herself. Mother lies down where it is wet and moves the child to where it is dry. Her two breasts satisfy its hunger and thirst; her sleeves shield it from wind and cold. In her tenderness she seldom uses a pillow; only when the child smiles is she glad. As long as the child is comfortable, the mother seeks no comfort for herself.
bm08.commentary: When the child wets the bed, the mother lies in the wet place and lays the child in the dry place. The Korean song line "she changed the wet place for a dry one" refers to exactly this kindness.

bm09.heading: Sixth, the Kindness of Nursing and Raising
bm09.plain: Sixth, the kindness of nursing and raising the child. Mother is like the earth, father like the sky. As sky covers and earth carries with equal kindness, so it is with father and mother. They neither resent nor glare in anger, nor reject a child whose limbs are crooked. The child born of her own body she cherishes and adores all day long.
bm09.commentary: Father covers like the sky; mother supports like the earth. It sings of parents who love their child unconditionally, whatever the child is like.

bm10.heading: Seventh, the Kindness of Washing Away the Unclean
bm10.plain: Seventh, the kindness of washing what is soiled. Remember how lovely her face once was, how graceful her bearing. Her brows had the color of green willows, her cheeks were redder than lotuses. Her deep kindness wore away that jade-like face; washing roughened her fine hands. Only out of love for her sons and daughters did a mother's face change.
bm10.commentary: Washing her children's diapers and clothes, a once young and beautiful mother grows old. This is one of the most heartrending verses to read.

bm11.heading: Eighth, the Kindness of Worrying When the Child Travels Far
bm11.plain: Eighth, the kindness of worrying when the child goes far away. Parting at death is truly hard to bear, and parting in life is painful too. When the child goes beyond distant mountains, the mother thinks of the child in a strange land. Day and night her heart follows, and thousands of tears flow, like a monkey weeping for its lost young, her insides breaking inch by inch.
bm11.commentary: It borrows an old story of a mother monkey who wept to death for her lost young; when she was opened, her insides were found broken in pieces. It is a mother's heartbreak as she longs for a child who has gone away.

bm12.heading: Ninth, the Kindness of Deep Care and Understanding
bm12.plain: Ninth, the kindness of caring with deep understanding. Parents' love is weighty, their kindness so deep that it is truly hard to repay. They wish to bear their child's pain in its place; when the child toils, the mother has no peace. Hearing the child is setting out on a long journey, she worries it will sleep in the cold at night. Even a brief hardship for her son or daughter leaves her heart aching long.
bm12.commentary: In some editions this kindness is called "the kindness of even doing wrong for the child's sake." It is the heart of parents willing to carry anything for their child.

bm13.heading: Tenth, the Kindness of Lifelong Compassion
bm13.plain: Tenth, the kindness of compassion to the very end. Parents' kindness is deep and weighty; their tender care never rests. Rising or sitting, their hearts follow the child; near or far, their thoughts go with it. Even at a hundred, a mother still worries about her eighty-year-old child. Would you know when this love and kindness end? Only when life ends do they part.
bm13.commentary: "Even at a hundred, a mother worries about her eighty-year-old child" is the best-known line of this sutra. Parents' love does not end even when the child grows old; it lasts until their life ends.

bm14.heading: A Kindness That Cannot Be Repaid
bm14.plain: The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Suppose someone carried their father on the left shoulder and their mother on the right, and walked around Mount Sumeru for a hundred thousand kalpas until their skin wore through to the bone and the bone wore through to the marrow, and blood flowed until it covered their ankles. Even so, they could not repay the deep kindness of their parents."
bm14.commentary: Even circling the world's greatest mountain endlessly with one's parents on one's shoulders cannot repay their kindness. Only when we know how great it is does the wish to repay it arise.

bm15.heading: The Way to Repay Their Kindness
bm15.plain: The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If you wish to repay their kindness, copy this sutra for your parents, read and recite this sutra for your parents, repent of your wrongs for your parents, make offerings to the Three Jewels for your parents, receive and keep the precepts for your parents, and give and make merit for your parents. Whoever can do this may be called a devoted child."
bm15.commentary: Six ways are given to repay a kindness that cannot be repaid. Each one is doing good "for your parents." Reading, listening to and copying the sutras in this app can also be dedicated as merit for your parents.

gridhrakuta.definition: Gṛdhrakūṭa, a mountain near Rājagṛha where the Buddha often taught.

ananda.definition: The Buddha's cousin and attendant. Having heard more teachings than anyone at the Buddha's side, he is called "foremost in hearing."

three-realms.definition: The three realms are the worlds beings live in (desire, form, formlessness); the four births are the ways all life is born (from womb, egg, moisture, transformation). Together they mean all beings.

sumeru.definition: In Buddhist cosmology, the highest and greatest mountain, rising at the center of the world.

three-jewels.definition: The three treasures of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community of practitioners).
